# Repeat: null distributions and the thousand-test trap {#sec-repeat}
::: {.callout-warning title="Under construction"}
<!-- banner:under-construction -->
This chapter is drafted but **not yet instructor-reviewed**. Content may change without

## The problem

The methylation project from @sec-simulating-a-process has grown. Your collaborator now has
**1,200 CpG sites** measured in **30 tumor samples and 30 normal samples**, with a read count and
a methylated fraction at every site in every sample. Each of those measurements is the one you
built in chapter 1. She wants the sites where tumor and normal genuinely differ, because the
top of that list gets validated by pyrosequencing at real cost per site.

She has already looked, and the differences are *everywhere*: almost no site shows exactly the
same fraction in both groups. Chapter 1 explains why. Two groups of thirty samples differ at every
site by sampling variability alone, even where the biology is identical.

All 1,200 sites differ, so the question worth asking is a narrower one: **which differences are
larger than two identical groups would show, and what happens to the answers when you ask that
question 1,200 times.**

## The story

Chapter 1 called the thing you built a *world*: a story of how the data came to be, written as
code you can run, with the truth as an input. The word for that is a **model** — a deliberately
simplified version of a process, built so you can run it and ask what it produces. Every world
you built in @sec-simulating-a-process was one, and *model* is the word from here on.

This unit's operation is **repeat**, and it is built from parts you already have. One site is
chapter 1's story told twice: tumor's true fraction $m$ and normal's true fraction $m$, each
observed through finite reads in finite samples. The two fractions are the same $m$, because the
model being built here is the one in which nothing is going on. The whole experiment is that
story repeated 1,200 times, one $m$ per site, spread across the genome's range.

The model in which nothing is going on is called the **null model**, and this unit's work is
building it explicitly, as code you can run. It answers a question her real data cannot: what do
purely accidental differences look like, at this depth, with these group sizes, across this many
sites? Her observed differences are then compared against the ones the null model produces.

## The story, as code

Repeating the story from @sec-simulating-a-process two thousand times per site, across 1,200
sites, is slow with the loops you hand-built there. Three new tools do the same jobs in one
call each:

```{python}
import numpy as np

values = [0.6, 0.7, 0.5, 0.7]
arr = np.array(values)             # arithmetic acts on every element at once
print(arr / 2)
print(arr.mean(), arr.std())       # chapter 1's average() and spread(), as built-ins
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
print(rng.binomial(80, 0.65, 5))   # five sequencing runs in one call
print(rng.uniform(0.2, 0.8, 5))    # five methylation levels, anywhere between 0.2 and 0.8
```

`np.array` turns a list into an **array**, and arithmetic on an array applies to every element
without a loop. The **reductions** `.mean()`, `.std()`, and `.sum()` collapse an array to one
number, which is what `average()` and `spread()` did in @sec-simulating-a-process, now at machine
speed. `rng.binomial(n, m, size)` runs the per-read loop from that chapter as a single call, one
whole experiment per draw. `rng.uniform(low, high, size)` extends chapter 1's `rng.random()` —
*a number anywhere between 0 and 1, every value equally likely* — to run between `low` and `high`
and to return `size` of them at once.

The two draw different things. `binomial` draws *counts* out of a process whose $m$ you supplied.
`uniform` draws *values of $m$ itself*, spread evenly across a range with no value favored, which
is how every site below gets its own methylation level. The statistics are unchanged from chapter
1; only the speed is different.

The next chunk computes one site's group difference, then 1,200 of them. The inner function is
chapter 1's simulator written in the built-in form.

```{python}
def group_fraction(m, n_samples, n_reads, rng):
    """Average observed methylation across one group's samples."""
    counts = rng.binomial(n_reads, m, n_samples)   # one methylated-read count per sample
    fractions = counts / n_reads
    return fractions.mean()

def null_scan(site_truths, n_samples, n_reads, rng):
    """Observed tumor-minus-normal difference at every site, when NO site truly differs."""
    diffs = []
    for m in site_truths:
        tumor = group_fraction(m, n_samples, n_reads, rng)
        normal = group_fraction(m, n_samples, n_reads, rng)
        diffs.append(tumor - normal)
    return np.array(diffs)

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
truths = rng.uniform(0.2, 0.8, 1200)        # each site its own methylation level...
diffs = null_scan(truths, 30, 25, rng)      # ...identical in both groups
print(f"largest difference the null model produces: {np.abs(diffs).max():.3f}")
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "1,200 tumor-minus-normal differences from the null model, in which no site truly differs. Every difference shown is sampling variability."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.hist(diffs, bins=40, color="#2a78d6")
ax.set_xlabel("observed difference in methylation fraction (tumor − normal)")
ax.set_ylabel("sites")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

Every difference in that histogram was produced by a model in which no site truly differs. Some
of those sites differ by a full eight points of methylation, which is a difference a reasonable
person would call "clearly higher in tumor" on meeting it one at a time.

The histogram is a **null distribution**: the set of results a null model produces when you run
it, here 1,200 differences from a model in which no site differs. Each observed difference in her
data is compared against a distribution of this kind.

Three terms are worth separating, because a statistics course introduces them in a different
order. The **null hypothesis** is the claim that nothing is going on, stated in words. The null
model is that claim written as code you can run. The null distribution is what comes out when you
run it. A course would give you a formula for the distribution; here you obtain it by running the
model, which works for any story you can write down.

## Playing with the story

Pick one site and make the question precise. Say its observed difference is 0.045, and ask
whether that is surprising. Run *that site's* null model many times to obtain its own null
distribution, then count how often the null model produces a difference at least that big. Count
it in either direction, because a difference of −0.045 is exactly as extreme as +0.045.

```{python}
def null_differences(m, n_sims, rng):
    """Many runs of one site's null model: same true m for both groups."""
    diffs = []
    for _ in range(n_sims):
        tumor = group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng)
        normal = group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng)
        diffs.append(tumor - normal)
    return np.array(diffs)

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
m, observed = 0.5, 0.045
null = null_differences(m, 2000, rng)
at_least_as_extreme = np.abs(null) >= abs(observed)   # True/False per run, either direction
p = at_least_as_extreme.mean()                        # fraction of True = the p-value
print(f"nothing produces a difference ≥ {observed} about {p:.1%} of the time")
```

That fraction is the **p-value**: the share of the null distribution at least as extreme as the
observation. It is around 8% here, which makes the observed difference mildly unusual, of a size
the null model produces a few times in every hundred runs.

**Predict before running.** Compute the p-value for all 1,200 sites of the null model and
histogram the results. What shape appears? The answer is exact rather than approximate, so work
it out from what a p-value of 0.30 means and how often the null model produces a result its own
top 30% exceeds.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "P-values for 1,200 sites where nothing is going on. The distribution is flat, which is what an honest test produces under the null."
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
pvals = np.empty(1200)
for i, m in enumerate(truths):
    obs = group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng) - group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng)
    null = null_differences(m, 300, rng)
    pvals[i] = np.mean(np.abs(null) >= abs(obs))   # the p-value, as above

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8))
ax.hist(pvals, bins=20, color="#2a78d6")
ax.axhline(60, color="#52514e", ls=":", lw=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("p-value")
ax.set_ylabel("sites")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
print(f"sites with p < 0.05: {(pvals < 0.05).sum()} of 1200")
```

The histogram is flat by construction. A p-value of 0.05 means the null model produces a result
that extreme 5% of the time, so under the null 5% of p-values land below 0.05, 10% below 0.10,
and so on for every threshold.

Flatness has a direct consequence for a large scan. In a scan with nothing to find, at
the conventional p < 0.05, **dozens of sites come up "significant"**: 56 in the run above,
against the $1200 \times 0.05 = 60$ the arithmetic gives. Nothing is wrong with the test. The
cause is that an honest 1-in-20 question was asked 1,200 times.

### One direction or two? {#sec-rep-sides}

Every p-value above counted the null runs at least as extreme as the observation, and one line of
code decided what "extreme" meant: `np.abs(null) >= abs(obs)` — *a run counts if it is as far from
zero as the observation, in either direction*. The result is the **two-sided** p-value, and it
answers the question "does this site differ?"

A second, narrower question is "is tumor *higher* at this site?" Its p-value counts only the runs
that exceed the observation upward, and it is called a **one-sided** p-value. The chunk below
reads the same 2,000 null runs both ways.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The same 2,000 null runs, read two ways. Colored bars are the runs each p-value counts; the dotted line is the observed 0.045."
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
m, observed = 0.5, 0.045
null = null_differences(m, 2000, rng)                # the same 2,000 runs as above

both_tails = np.abs(null) >= abs(observed)           # True where either direction is as extreme
upper_tail = null >= observed                        # True only where "tumor higher" is as extreme
print(f"two-sided p = {both_tails.mean():.1%}   one-sided p = {upper_tail.mean():.1%}")
print(f"one-sided p, had the site gone the other way by 0.045: {np.mean(null >= -observed):.1%}")

def tail_plot(ax, mask, title):
    """Every null run in gray, then the runs this p-value counts in color."""
    edges = np.linspace(-0.1, 0.1, 41)
    ax.hist(null, bins=edges, color="#c9c7c3")
    ax.hist(null[mask], bins=edges, color="#eb6834")
    ax.axvline(observed, color="#52514e", ls=":", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("difference (tumor − normal)")
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 2.8), sharey=True)
tail_plot(left, both_tails, "two-sided: both tails count")
tail_plot(right, upper_tail, "one-sided: only \"tumor higher\" counts")
left.set_ylabel("runs")
plt.show()
```

The one-sided p-value is almost exactly half the two-sided one, 4.2% against 8.6%. The cause is
that the null model is symmetric: it overshoots upward about as often as downward, and the
one-sided count ignores the downward half.

Halving the p-value has two effects, and they are consequences of the same arithmetic. A
one-sided test has more power in the direction it was aimed, so the same observation clears
p < 0.05 one-sided and fails it two-sided. It also reports nothing in the other direction. Had
this site gone the other way by the same 0.045, the "tumor higher" p-value would be about 96%.

Both versions are honest under the null. Run either over the 1,200 nothing-sites and the
histogram is flat, because the one-sided version spends its whole 5% on one tail rather than
splitting it between two. What makes a one-sided p-value legitimate is *when the direction was
chosen*. The reason must come from outside the data, as when a CpG sits in a promoter known to
gain methylation in tumors and the only question worth asking is "higher?", and it must be
written down before the difference is computed. Both tests are fair when the direction is fixed
in advance, and the two-sided version is the default because it needs no such justification. The
cost of picking the direction *after* seeing which way the difference went is measured later in
this chapter.

## Where the numbers come from

Now build her actual situation: a model in which most sites are null and a few are not. Sixty
sites have tumor running 0.07 higher, among 1,140 where nothing happens. You know which sites are
which, because you set them. The chunk below runs the identical analysis and grades the discovery
list against that known truth.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The discovery list, graded against the truth only the simulator knows."
rng = np.random.default_rng(19)
base = rng.uniform(0.2, 0.8, 1200)
n_true, delta = 60, 0.07                     # sites 0..59 truly differ
pvals = np.empty(1200)
for i, m in enumerate(base):
    if i < n_true:
        m_tumor = m + delta        # one of the 60 sites that truly differ
    else:
        m_tumor = m                # nothing going on at this site
    obs = group_fraction(m_tumor, 30, 25, rng) - group_fraction(m, 30, 25, rng)
    null = null_differences(m, 300, rng)
    pvals[i] = np.mean(np.abs(null) >= abs(obs))

hits = pvals < 0.05
real, false = hits[:n_true].sum(), hits[n_true:].sum()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.6))
ax.barh(["false discoveries", "real discoveries"], [false, real],
        color=["#eb6834", "#2a78d6"])
for y, v in enumerate([false, real]):
    ax.text(v + 1.5, y, str(v), va="center")
ax.set_xlabel("sites reported at p < 0.05")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
print(f"list: {hits.sum()} sites — {real} real, {false} false — {false/hits.sum():.0%} of the list is noise")
```

The scan found most of the real sites, and **almost half the list is false**. Those false
discoveries are the accidents the flat histogram implies, in about the number the arithmetic
gives. Every p-value did what it claims, and the list is still half noise, because real effects
were rare and questions were plentiful: 60 truths cannot outnumber the accidents that 1,140 null
sites generate at 1-in-20.

The fraction of the reported list that is noise is the number her pyrosequencing budget depends
on, and it depends on two things rather than one. The threshold is one. The other is **how rare
true effects are**, which nobody knows in advance. Tighten the threshold to p < 0.01 and the
accidents drop toward eleven while most real sites survive. Every threshold trades real
discoveries kept against false ones admitted, and defending that trade is part of reporting the
list.

## The notation

This unit introduces two pieces of shorthand. The first states the p-value precisely:

> *the p-value is the probability that the null model produces a result at least as extreme as
> the one observed.*

Each phrase in that sentence carries a specific meaning. *Null model* is the story of nothing
happening, built as code you can run. *At least as extreme* covers both directions, unless the
direction was fixed before looking, which is the distinction @sec-rep-sides draws. *Produces*
means you obtain the probability by running the model, which is how every p-value above was
computed.

The second is the accounting rule the graded list demonstrated:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\text{false positives}] = m_{\text{null}} \cdot \alpha
$$

The rule uses three symbols, each of which you have already used. $\alpha$ (alpha) is the
**threshold**, meaning the p-value below which you call a site significant. It was 0.05 in every
scan above, written as the `0.05` in `pvals < 0.05`.

$m_{\text{null}}$ is the **number of tests where the null model is the truth**, which is the
number of sites where nothing is going on: all 1,200 in the null scan, and 1,140 in the graded
list. The letter $m$ for a count of tests is standard in the multiple-testing literature, and it
collides with the methylation fraction $m$ in the code. The subscript is a reminder that this $m$
counts questions rather than molecules.

$\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\,]$ is the **expected value**, the long-run average of a quantity across
many runs of the model. It is what `.mean()` over many runs approximates. The flat histogram is
why the rule holds exactly here, since a fraction $\alpha$ of truly-null tests land below
$\alpha$.

The expected number of accidental discoveries is therefore the number of truly-null questions
times the threshold. In the graded list that is $1140 \times 0.05 = 57$, against the 50 false
discoveries the run actually produced.

You cannot know $m_{\text{null}}$ in her data. You do know that $m_{\text{null}}$ is at most the
number of tests, so $1200 \times 0.05 = 60$ is a ceiling on the accidents, and it is known before
any data arrives. Report a scan's list next to that ceiling.

## A worked design

> **The problem.** A water authority screens **200 wells** monthly for arsenic exceedance.
> The assay is noisy, so each well's monthly result is a measurement, not a verdict. This month
> **9 wells exceeded** the threshold; last month it was 6; the month before, 7. Remediation means
> excavating a well at significant cost, and false alarms burn community trust. The board asks:
> **is contamination spreading, and which specific wells should we dig up?**

**Frame.** The board's sentence contains two questions, and they need different methods. "Is it
spreading" is a question about the *count*: is 9-of-200 surprising, given assay noise and each
well's history? "Which wells" is 200 individual questions asked simultaneously, so this month's
scan is a 200-test experiment in which some exceedances are the assay's accidents. I am treating
wells as independent for the count question, and flagging now that they are not. Wells share
aquifers, and neighboring wells' results move together, which makes a cluster of exceedances both
more suspicious as contamination and more producible by shared noise.

**Decompose.** (1) From each well's history, a null model: assay noise around that well's
ordinary level. (2) The count question: simulate 200 wells' ordinary months, count exceedances,
locate 9 in that distribution. (3) The which-wells question: per-well p-values, read against the
expected number of accidents — with 200 wells at a 3% accident rate, six exceedances is the
*baseline*, not a signal. (4) A decision rule that prices the asymmetry between the two
errors, since digging up a
clean well costs money and missing a contaminated one costs health. The threshold follows from
that comparison rather than from convention.

**Select.** The method must produce per-well evidence and the scan-wide accident count, and it
must let the board move the threshold and watch both costs respond, because the board needs to
set the threshold rather than receive a verdict. Forward simulation from each well's own history
does all three. The alternative I am not taking is flagging wells above a fixed concentration
cutoff, which is simpler and easier to audit. It fails because wells differ in baseline and in
assay noise, so a single cutoff is strict for clean wells and blind for dirty ones.

**Anticipate.** Three ways the answer could be wrong, and how I would find out.

First, each well's "ordinary level" comes from its own history. If a well has been contaminated
throughout that history, the history *is* the contamination, so the contaminated level becomes
the null model's baseline and the well becomes invisible to the analysis. I would check every
well whose baseline sits near the health limit against that absolute standard, and not only
against its own past.

Second, the aquifer correlation I set aside. A month of shared noise produces a cluster of
exceedances, and a count question that assumes independent wells reads that cluster as spreading
contamination. Before alarming the board I would ask whether this month's 9 wells share a water
table.

Third, 9 versus 6 versus 7 is three months of a count whose ordinary variation I have not
measured. The trend question may be unanswerable this early, and reporting that it is
unanswerable is itself a finding.

## When the model is wrong

Box's warning from @sec-simulating-a-process applies to the null model in particular. Everything
the scan concluded rests on the null model being the right model of "nothing going on," and there
are three ways it can fail to be.

**Choosing the direction after seeing the data nearly doubles the accident rate.** Suppose an
analyst computes a one-directional p-value, and picks the direction after looking at which way
the difference went. Each test still looks individually defensible. The chunk below measures what
the accident rate actually becomes.

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(23)
flagged = 0
for _ in range(2000):
    obs = group_fraction(0.5, 30, 25, rng) - group_fraction(0.5, 30, 25, rng)
    null = null_differences(0.5, 200, rng)
    if obs > 0:                          # direction chosen after looking:
        p = np.mean(null >= obs)         #   the difference went up, so test "up"
    else:
        p = np.mean(null <= obs)         #   the difference went down, so test "down"
    if p < 0.05:
        flagged += 1
print(f"accident rate with direction-after-looking: {flagged/2000:.3f}  (honest target: 0.05)")
```

With perfectly continuous measurements the rate is exactly double, and the discreteness of
counts recovers a little of it here. No single computation in the loop is wrong. What is wrong is
the model of the *procedure*: the direction was chosen using the data, so the question asked
depended on the answer. The same failure takes other forms — a threshold, a subgroup, or an
outcome chosen after looking — and together they are among the most common ways honest analysts
produce false discoveries.

**The 1,200 questions are not 1,200 independent questions.** Methylation comes in coordinated
regions, so neighboring CpG sites tend to move together, in the same way that neighboring
positions on a chromosome are inherited together (geneticists call that *linkage*). The null
model here drew every site independently.

Correlation leaves each individual p-value correct and changes what a *list* means. A run of ten
significant neighbors may be a single biological event reported ten times, and the accident count
varies far more between scans than the independent-sites arithmetic predicts. When discoveries
arrive in clusters, count events rather than tests.

**The null model's noise may be too small.** This chapter built "nothing going on" as one true
fraction per site with read-sampling variability only. Real samples vary for more reasons than
reads, including sample handling, cell composition and day-to-day effects, so the real null
distribution is *wider* than the one simulated here. Every accident count above is therefore a
floor rather than an estimate. @sec-nest takes up what happens when the truth itself varies under
the null, and how much that widening changes a scan like this one.

## Practice problems

Ungraded, solutions worked. Do them before looking.

### 2.1 · Predict the output {#sec-rep-p1}

A null scan of **5,000** sites, same settings as the chapter. Before running anything: what
shape is the p-value histogram, how many sites land below p = 0.01, and below p = 0.05?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Flat, with about **50** below 0.01 and about **250** below 0.05. No simulation is needed: under
the null, p-values are uniform, so the expected count below $\alpha$ is $5000\alpha$. A related
fact is worth remembering. If a scan of real data shows a flat histogram with a spike near zero,
the spike's excess over flat is a first estimate of how much true signal the scan contains.
:::

### 2.2 · Modify the story {#sec-rep-2}

Rebuild the graded-list experiment with **90 samples per group** instead of 30. Before running:
which numbers in the list composition change, in which direction — and which number provably
does not move?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Power rises. Group means tighten threefold in variance, so the 0.07 shifts stand out further and
essentially all 60 true sites are caught. The false-positive count **does not move**, because
truly-null sites produce p < 0.05 five percent of the time at any sample size. Larger samples
make real effects easier to detect and leave the accident rate where it was. The list therefore
improves in composition, at roughly 60 real against ~57 accidents, while the accidents themselves
remain. The two things that change the false count are the threshold and the number of null
questions asked.
:::

### 2.3 · Hand-calculate {#sec-rep-p3}

Five honest tests, all null, threshold 0.05. By hand: the probability that *at least one* comes
up significant. Then: the expected number that do.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Each test stays quiet with probability 0.95, so all five stay quiet with probability
$0.95^5 \approx 0.774$, and at least one fires with probability $1 - 0.774 = \mathbf{0.226}$.
Five questions therefore carry a 22.6% chance of at least one false positive. The expected
count is $5 \times 0.05 = 0.25$. Both numbers follow from multiplying the same two facts, with no
simulation and no software, and they extend by hand: at 100 tests, at least one false positive is
nearly certain, at $1 - 0.95^{100} \approx 0.994$.
:::

### 2.4 · Spot the mismatch {#sec-rep-p4}

A paper reports: *"Of 12,000 genes tested, 640 reached p < 0.05. Since chance predicts 600, we
identified 40 genes whose expression truly changed."* The arithmetic is right. What is wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
The subtraction is performed on *counts*, and the claim is made about *genes*. Nothing in the
analysis connects the two levels. An excess of 40 over the expected 600 is weak evidence that
some signal exists somewhere in the scan, but the 640 names on the list are approximately 600
accidents and 40 truths shuffled together, and the analysis contains no step that distinguishes
them. "We identified 40 genes" claims an identification that was never performed. An honest
version reads: "the excess suggests on the order of 40 real changes; individually, no gene on
this list is more than about 6% likely to be one of them without further evidence."
:::

### 2.5 · Read the notation {#sec-rep-p5}

Translate $\mathbb{E}[\text{FP}] = m_{\text{null}}\,\alpha$ into one line of code for a 20,000-gene
scan at $\alpha = 0.01$, and one sentence for a collaborator deciding whether to trust a
180-gene discovery list from that scan.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
```{python}
print(20000 * 0.01)
```
Sentence: "even if nothing in your experiment changed, this scan produces about 200 genes at
p < 0.01, so a 180-gene list is fewer discoveries than the null model typically produces on its
own. The list is not yet evidence of anything, and it needs a different threshold or a different
design before anyone spends money on it."
:::
